messages.subject: Re: [canopy_phylogeny] Falcon-X site biases
messages.body_plain:
Hi Katherine,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy and Falcon-X. Briefly, the site specific bias is obtained using CODEX, where the coverage is the total read depth at the germline heterozygous loci, the GC content is calculated from a 50bp window centered at each locus. More details on the method side can be found here https://www.e-publications.org/ims/submission/AOAS/user/submissionFile/25603?confirm=c52a45d8, which is our publication in AOAS.

We are in the process of generating more detailed user instructions for Canopy and will include Falcon-X for allele-specific copy numbers. Currently the demonstration on how to generate CNA input is by Sequenza (https://github.com/yuchaojiang/Canopy/blob/master/instruction/SNA_CNA_input.md ). We are aiming at releasing/updating the manual later this week / early next week. Please visit our GitHub page sometime mid next week!

Yuchao

messages.subject: Are parameters determined subjectively or objectively?
messages.subject_clean: Are parameters determined subjectively or objectively?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yuchao,
     Canopy appears to be a very powerful tool and I am eager to apply it to my collection of paired local/disseminated tumor samples. I am most interested in generating phylogenetic trees. Before getting started I have a question which may simply reflect the fact that I am relatively new to this type of analysis using R. I have successfully gone through the Toy examples, though that was relatively simple since the values were provided.

      Are the values for K (range for number of subclones), numchain (number of chains with random iterations), and num_cluster determined empirically/objectively (i.e using PyClone to determine number of mutation clusters) or do you have to use trial and error to select them? If I'm correct, the BIC tells you the optimal number of subclones, and the user selects the tree determined to have the highest posterior likelihood. Also, the burnin and the thin are to be modified by the user as needed.

 With approximately 20 replicates (10 local, 10 disseminated) for some cases, do I go over my data beforehand to generate a rough estimate for subclone number and then apply a range for K?
Also, is it necessary to run a "normal" or germline control?

Thanks for your help.

Rob

messages.subject: Re: [canopy_phylogeny] Are parameters determined subjectively or objectively?
messages.subject_clean: [canopy_phylogeny] Are parameters determined subjectively or objectively?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy and sorry for my late reply.

The value for K will be determined by BIC as a model selection metric.

Numchain is the number of MCMC chains with random starts so that the samplings won’t get stuck in a local mode. The value for numchain is user-defined. We recommend a large value so that the MCMC will converge. In the most recent push, the MCMC has a check so that it can stop once it has converged based on acceptance rate and posterior likelihood.

Num_cluster is only used in clustering of SNAs, which is a by-product of Canopy. It is a range and again model selection will be used to determine the optimal value. Sometimes visual guidance can help so that a fixed scalar num_cluster can be used as input for clustering.

Burnin and thinning parameters are user defined as well based on how long MCMC is run. A plot of posterior likelihood will be generated by Canopy before thinning and binning. You can refer to the plot to determine these parameters. Note that the writeskip parameter skips trees for storage (so that it doesn’t eat up too much RAM) which essentially is thinning while sampling. Therefore, for thinning, you don’t need a large value.

For the 10 local + 10 disseminated cases, I’m not sure what’s your plan to “go over your data beforehand to generate a rough estimate of number of subclones” but if you can that certainly would help Canopy perform better. With this said, I don’t think Canopy is able to detect a large number of subclones (usually < = 6) especially with two bulk sequencing (assuming each replicate can be different from a different model organism).

To run a normal or germline control is recommended so that you can accurately call somatic SNVs and profile CNAs. These upstream processing isn’t the focus of Canopy yet they are very important. You can refer to our GitHub page under common questions for details on how to generate a clean set of SNV and CNA input for Canopy.

Hope that this helps and feel free to let me know if you have further questions.

Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: Canopy CCF
messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

Glad Canopy is working well! Sorry for my late reply — I just got back from travels. Please see my response below.

Hope this helps and feel free to let us know if you have further questions.

Yuchao

> On May 23, 2017, at 6:46 AM, Rodney, Simon <s.ro...@ucl.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> Dear Yuchao,
>
> Thank you for your previous assistance with Canopy – it is now working great for me and I look forward to citing it in future papers of ours.
>
> We have two hopefully quick questions which we would really appreciate your advise on.
> From Canopy’s output Is there a quick way to calculate the cancer cell fraction or mutant cell frequency for each cluster clone?
>

This is a great question. I don’t think Canopy has this output at this stage. However, it is easy to get since we know the position of the mutations along the tree branches and we know the clonal frequencies (i.e., the composition of the clones for the tumor samples, which is the P matrix in our notation.) I will push an update on this soon to our GitHub page.

> Also if there is an allele specific copy number amplification how does one know if an SNA in that region is on that allele or not?
>

If the SNA happens after the CNA change or if the SNA is on a separate linage from the CNA, then it doesn’t matter since only one allele will be mutated. If an SNA happens before the CNA, then we need to know whether the mutated allele gets amplified or not if it is a duplication CNA event following that. We think this is the biologically interesting scenario since a lot studies have shown deleterious point mutations undergo copy-neutral LOH events and thus have a two copy enrichment. In this case, the H vector tells whether the SNA is in the major copy or not after the CNA event. The H vector is stored within each tree list after posterior evaluation. For example, below is a tree that is pre-stored as part of our Canopy package.

library(Canopy)
data("MDA231_tree")
MDA231_tree$H

>
> Many thanks,
>
> Simon
>
> Dr Simon Rodney
> UCL Cancer Institute
